question.prompt: Which receiver-facing guarantee should be authoritative? This determines whether retries after a lost acknowledgement may repeat a successfully processed request and what receivers must deduplicate.

options.label: At-least-once (Recommended)
options.description: Retry ambiguous outcomes and require receivers to deduplicate using a stable event or delivery identifier; duplicates are possible, but silent loss is minimized.

options.label: At-most-once
options.description: Do not retry ambiguous outcomes, preventing sender-created duplicates but allowing events to be permanently lost when acknowledgements disappear.

options.label: Configurable per endpoint
options.description: Let each endpoint choose at-least-once or at-most-once behavior, increasing flexibility but materially expanding API, persistence, UI, testing, and support complexity.

question.prompt: Which identifier must receivers use to deduplicate automatic retries? This determines the persistence uniqueness rules and whether a lost acknowledgement can safely trigger the same logical delivery again.

options.label: Stable delivery ID
options.description: Assign one delivery ID per event-endpoint pair and reuse it across every automatic attempt, while also exposing a separate stable event ID for business correlation.

options.label: Stable event ID
options.description: Require deduplication by event ID across endpoints, which is simpler but can incorrectly collapse intentionally distinct subscriptions or endpoint configurations.

options.label: Unique attempt ID
options.description: Give every retry a new receiver-visible identity, preserving attempt traceability but providing no reliable key for suppressing duplicate processing.

answer: Receivers must deduplicate automatic retries using the stable Webhook-Id event UUID, scoped by sender tenant identifier. The same Webhook-Id is preserved across all automatic attempts, endpoints, endpoint changes, and manual replays; sender-side delivery identity remains separately keyed by event ID and endpoint ID.

question.prompt: When an account event is accepted, what endpoint state should be frozen for its automatic deliveries? This determines whether later endpoint edits or rotations can redirect or alter already-queued requests.

options.label: Freeze full delivery config
options.description: Snapshot eligible endpoint IDs, destination URLs, and signing-key versions per delivery; later changes affect only new events, giving queued deliveries deterministic behavior.

options.label: Freeze membership only
options.description: Snapshot which endpoints receive the event but resolve their current URL and signing configuration at attempt time, allowing edits to affect queued deliveries.

options.label: Resolve everything later
options.description: Workers use endpoint membership and configuration current at execution time, reducing snapshots but allowing edits or disablement to change event fanout.

answer: Freeze full delivery config. When the account event is accepted, snapshot each eligible endpoint’s immutable endpoint ID, destination URL, and signing-key version into its event-and-endpoint delivery record. Automatic attempts and their scheduling use that snapshot, so later endpoint edits, deletion, or signing-key rotation affect only deliveries created for new events and cannot redirect or alter an already-queued delivery. Endpoint disablement is the exception: it cancels that endpoint’s scheduled future attempts without deleting or rewriting existing delivery or attempt history. Manual replay remains linked to the original delivery and event ID but creates a new run using the endpoint configuration and active signing key selected at replay initiation; that replay configuration is then frozen for the run and displayed in history.

question.prompt: Which signing mechanism should be authoritative? This security-sensitive choice determines how receivers authenticate the exact request and how signing keys are stored and rotated.

options.label: Versioned HMAC-SHA256
options.description: Sign an unambiguous byte sequence containing the timestamp, sender tenant ID, Webhook-Id, and exact raw JSON body using the snapshotted secret version; simple and broadly interoperable, but each receiver holds a symmetric secret.

options.label: Ed25519 signatures
options.description: Sign the same canonical inputs with a private key and let receivers keep only public keys; improves verifier-side secret safety but adds asymmetric-key distribution and operational complexity.

options.label: HTTP Message Signatures
options.description: Adopt the standards-based HTTP signature framework for covered components and body integrity; most extensible, but substantially more complex for receiver implementations and interoperability testing.

answer: Versioned HMAC-SHA256

question.prompt: What exact byte sequence must HMAC-SHA256 cover? This determines whether independent receiver implementations can verify the request without JSON reserialization or ambiguous field boundaries.

options.label: Framed metadata + body
options.description: Sign a versioned, length-framed sequence containing timestamp, sender tenant ID, Webhook-Id, and the exact transmitted body bytes; strongest unambiguous binding with modest receiver complexity.

options.label: Timestamp + raw body
options.description: Sign the timestamp followed by a delimiter and exact body bytes; simpler and familiar, but tenant and Webhook-Id headers are not independently authenticated unless duplicated in the body.

options.label: Canonicalized JSON
options.description: Sign a canonical JSON representation containing metadata and payload; human-readable but requires every receiver SDK to implement identical canonicalization.

answer: Send the exact persisted UTF-8 JSON byte sequence as the HTTP body without reserialization or content encoding. HMAC-SHA256 must cover the ASCII value of Webhook-Id, followed by a period byte (0x2E), the ASCII base-10 Unix-seconds value of Webhook-Timestamp, another period byte, and the exact transmitted body bytes: Webhook-Id + "." + Webhook-Timestamp + "." + body. Header values are not trimmed or normalized.

question.prompt: Which HTTP outcome policy should be authoritative? This determines when a receiver may see the same Webhook-Id again and when a delivery becomes terminal.

options.label: Conservative transient set
options.description: Treat any network error or timeout as ambiguous and retry; accept only 200–299; retry 408, 425, 429, and 500–599; treat other 300–499 responses as terminal; never follow redirects; honor bounded Retry-After before exponential backoff.

options.label: All non-2xx retry
options.description: Retry every response outside 200–299, maximizing recovery from receiver mistakes but wasting capacity on permanent failures and potentially retrying redirects or authorization errors indefinitely.

options.label: 5xx and network only
options.description: Retry network errors, timeouts, and 500–599 only; treat all 300–499 responses as terminal, simplifying behavior but potentially dropping recoverable throttling and timeout responses.

answer: Use the conservative transient set. Each endpoint delivery has at most 6 automatic attempts including the initial attempt. Connection refusal, DNS failure, connect timeout, TLS failure, response timeout, HTTP 408, HTTP 425, HTTP 429, and HTTP 5xx consume an attempt and are retryable. Other HTTP 4xx responses consume an attempt and immediately make the delivery terminally failed. A complete 2xx response makes it succeeded. Redirects are not followed and are treated as terminal 4xx-class failures. Retryable outcomes schedule delays of 10, 30, 120, 600, and 3600 seconds after attempts 1 through 5, measured from completion of the preceding attempt. For 429 or 503, a valid Retry-After value replaces the scheduled delay only when it is between 1 and 3600 seconds; otherwise the normal delay applies. No seventh automatic attempt is created.

question.prompt: What ordering guarantee should each endpoint receive? This determines whether a retrying delivery blocks newer events and how much concurrency workers may use.

options.label: Unordered concurrent
options.description: Make no arrival-order guarantee and allow bounded concurrent deliveries per endpoint; maximizes throughput and avoids head-of-line blocking, while receivers must tolerate reordering.

options.label: Strict endpoint FIFO
options.description: Allow only one nonterminal automatic delivery per endpoint, so later events wait through all retries; simplest receiver ordering but one failing event can block the endpoint for over an hour.

options.label: Ordered first attempts
options.description: Start initial attempts in event order but allow retries to overlap newer events; reduces routine reordering but provides no strict processing-order guarantee and complicates the contract.

answer: Unordered concurrent

question.prompt: Which receiver-facing signature envelope should be authoritative? This determines interoperable verification, replay protection, tenant scoping, and how receivers select the snapshotted signing secret.

options.label: Explicit versioned headers
options.description: Send Webhook-Id, Webhook-Timestamp, Webhook-Tenant-Id, Webhook-Key-Version, and Webhook-Signature: v1=<lowercase hex HMAC>; require the tenant ID in the persisted JSON body, generate timestamp at each attempt, and require receivers to reject timestamps more than 5 minutes from their clock while still deduplicating by tenant ID plus Webhook-Id.

options.label: Compact signature header
options.description: Combine version, timestamp, key version, and signature into one structured Webhook-Signature header while keeping Webhook-Id and tenant ID separate; this reduces header count but requires a custom parser and duplicates timestamp handling less transparently.

options.label: Minimal headers
options.description: Expose only Webhook-Id, Webhook-Timestamp, and Webhook-Signature, requiring receivers to infer tenant and key selection from endpoint configuration; this is simpler but weakens multi-tenant routing and secret-rotation interoperability.

answer: Expose only Webhook-Id, Webhook-Timestamp, and Webhook-Signature. Webhook-Signature contains comma-separated v1=<lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256> entries. Require all three headers, generate a fresh timestamp and signature for every attempt, reject timestamps more than 300 seconds from receiver time, and accept the request if any v1 signature matches any currently accepted secret using constant-time comparison. Tenant identity and signing-key selection come from the endpoint configuration; no receiver-facing tenant or key-version header is authoritative.

question.prompt: During signing-secret rotation, which overlap model is authoritative? This determines whether queued deliveries signed under a frozen old key remain verifiable and how comma-separated v1 signatures are generated.

options.label: Dual-sign overlap
options.description: For a bounded rotation window, sign each attempt with both its snapshotted key and the endpoint’s active key, then retire the old key only after the window and all old-key deliveries are terminal; this eases receiver migration but requires protected access to both secrets.

options.label: Snapshot key only
options.description: Sign each automatic delivery only with its frozen key, requiring receivers to retain every old secret until all associated deliveries are terminal; simplest sender behavior but makes receiver rotation coordination stricter.

options.label: Active key only
options.description: Always sign attempts with the currently active key despite the delivery snapshot, simplifying receiver retention but contradicting the confirmed immutable signing configuration and changing queued deliveries after rotation.

answer: Use a 24-hour verification overlap, but do not dual-sign. Once rotation begins, every newly started attempt—including attempts for queued deliveries whose delivery record snapshots the old key version—is signed only with the new active secret. Receivers accept signatures from both the old and new secrets for 24 hours, after which the old secret is retired. Webhook-Signature therefore contains one v1 entry per attempt under normal rotation; comma-separated entries remain a verification format, not a requirement to emit both rotation keys. The delivery snapshot remains immutable historical configuration, while the rotation rule explicitly governs attempt-time signing.

question.prompt: Which outbound destination policy must webhook endpoints follow? This determines whether tenant-controlled URLs can reach internal infrastructure and what validation workers must repeat before every connection.

options.label: Public HTTPS only
options.description: Require HTTPS, block loopback/link-local/private/reserved IP ranges after DNS resolution, re-resolve and revalidate every attempt, connect only to the validated address, and continue to prohibit redirects; strongest production isolation with no private-network destinations.

options.label: Public HTTP or HTTPS
options.description: Apply the same IP and DNS-rebinding protections but permit plaintext HTTP, improving local compatibility while exposing webhook bodies and signatures to network interception.

options.label: Private destinations allowed
options.description: Permit private or internal addresses through explicit tenant allowlists, enabling intranet integrations but requiring materially broader network isolation, authorization, auditing, and support controls.

answer: Public HTTPS only. Webhook endpoint URLs must use HTTPS. On every delivery attempt, resolve the destination hostname, reject loopback, link-local, private, reserved, multicast, and otherwise non-public IP addresses, and connect only to the validated resolved address. Repeat DNS resolution and IP validation before every connection to prevent DNS rebinding. Do not follow redirects; treat them as terminal failures under the established outcome policy. Private or internal destinations and plaintext HTTP are not permitted.

question.prompt: What boundary makes an account event durably accepted for webhook delivery? This determines whether committing the business event and creating its webhook fanout must be atomic, and therefore whether the platform can promise not to miss committed events.

options.label: Transactional outbox
options.description: Commit the account event and an outbox record atomically in the same datastore, then asynchronously create snapshotted deliveries; strongest no-gap guarantee but requires integration with the business transaction.

options.label: Durable enqueue API

question.prompt: What should one manual replay create? This determines whether replay receives its own retry budget and history while deliberately reusing the original Webhook-Id, which may cause the receiver to suppress it as already processed.

options.label: New retry run

question.prompt: When a manual replay reuses an already processed Webhook-Id, what must receivers do? This determines whether replay can repeat business effects or is only a safe redelivery that receivers may suppress.

options.label: Deduplicate replay
options.description: Receivers apply the same tenant-plus-Webhook-Id deduplication to automatic attempts and manual replays; replay verifies transport and can recover only when the original event was not recorded as processed.

options.label: Process replay again
options.description: Receivers must distinguish a replay and intentionally process it again despite the reused Webhook-Id, requiring a new authenticated replay indicator and receiver-side safeguards.

options.label: Issue new ID
options.description: Manual replay receives a new Webhook-Id linked to the original, enabling ordinary processing but revising the confirmed rule that replays preserve the original identity.

answer: Receivers must apply the same sender-tenant-plus-Webhook-Id deduplication to manual replays as to automatic retries. Within the 30-day deduplication window, an already processed event must be suppressed and must not repeat business effects. After that window, a replay may be processed again and must be labeled as outside the promised deduplication window.

question.prompt: Which JSON envelope must every webhook use? This fixes the receiver contract and the immutable body bytes persisted and signed for all attempts and replays.

options.label: Versioned envelope
options.description: Use a stable envelope containing id, type, version, occurred_at, account_id, and data; evolve event payloads through explicit per-type integer versions while keeping the envelope backward compatible.

options.label: CloudEvents JSON
options.description: Adopt the structured CloudEvents JSON format and place the product payload in data; improves standards interoperability but adds a broader external specification and compatibility surface.

options.label: Event-specific body
options.description: Send each event's fields at the JSON root with only minimal shared metadata; produces smaller payloads but weakens uniform parsing and version evolution.

answer: Versioned envelope. Every webhook body is a stable UTF-8 JSON envelope containing id, type, version, occurred_at, account_id, and data. The id equals the immutable Webhook-Id UUID, type identifies the event type, version is an integer version scoped to that event type, occurred_at is the event occurrence timestamp, account_id identifies the sender tenant account, and data contains the event-specific payload. Envelope fields remain backward compatible, while incompatible event payload changes require a new per-type version. The exact serialized envelope bytes are persisted once and reused unchanged for every automatic attempt and manual replay.

question.prompt: If a signing secret is suspected compromised, what must emergency revocation do? This security-sensitive choice determines whether containment may interrupt deliveries instead of preserving the normal 24-hour verification overlap.

options.label: Revoke and pause
options.description: Immediately retire the compromised secret with no overlap, pause new attempts for the endpoint, and resume only after an authorized operator activates a replacement secret; strongest containment with explicit delivery interruption.

options.label: Rotate immediately
options.description: Immediately sign new attempts with a replacement secret but keep the compromised secret accepted for the normal 24-hour overlap; preserves availability but leaves the known-compromised verifier credential usable.

options.label: Revoke and continue
options.description: Immediately retire the compromised secret and continue signing with a newly generated secret without pausing; minimizes interruption but receivers may reject deliveries until they obtain the replacement.

answer: Immediately revoke the compromised secret with no 24-hour overlap, pause all new attempts for the affected endpoint, cancel its scheduled future attempts without deleting or rewriting history, and resume delivery only after an authorized operator activates a replacement secret. Existing delivery, replay-run, and attempt records remain immutable and auditable.

question.prompt: Who may view delivery history and initiate manual replay? This determines whether internal support can cause receiver-visible traffic and what authorization and audit controls are mandatory.

options.label: Tenant + break-glass support
options.description: Tenant admins may view and replay their account’s deliveries; scoped support may view redacted history and replay only through an explicit break-glass action requiring a reason and immutable audit record.

options.label: Tenant admins only
options.description: Only tenant administrators may view history or replay deliveries, minimizing internal privilege but limiting support’s ability to diagnose and recover incidents.

options.label: Tenant + full support
options.description: Tenant admins and authorized support staff may freely view details and replay deliveries within assigned tenants, improving support speed but increasing privilege and misuse risk.

answer: Tenant admins may view and replay their account’s deliveries. Authorized support staff with tenant-scoped access may view only redacted delivery history. Support-initiated replay requires an explicit break-glass action, a recorded reason, and an immutable audit record identifying the actor, tenant, delivery, replay run, and time.

question.prompt: How must endpoint fanout be captured when the business event commits? This decides whether the platform can guarantee that later endpoint edits cannot change which deliveries belong to an already accepted event.

options.label: Create deliveries atomically
options.description: In the same transaction as the event and outbox record, create one delivery per eligible endpoint with its frozen URL and configuration; strongest guarantee, but couples event commits to endpoint lookup and fanout writes.

options.label: Snapshot into outbox
options.description: Atomically store the complete eligible endpoint/configuration snapshot in the outbox, then let workers create delivery records from only that snapshot; preserves the guarantee with a larger outbox record and asynchronous materialization.

options.label: Resolve after commit
options.description: Store only the event, then resolve endpoints when the outbox is processed; simpler writes, but endpoint changes after acceptance can alter fanout and contradict the confirmed freeze-at-acceptance behavior.

answer: Create deliveries atomically. In the same datastore transaction that commits the business event and outbox record, create one delivery record for every endpoint eligible at that moment, with its immutable endpoint ID, destination URL, and applicable configuration frozen on the delivery. The transaction must fail as a unit if the complete fanout cannot be persisted. Later endpoint edits, deletion, or rotation must not add, remove, redirect, or otherwise alter deliveries belonging to the accepted event; endpoint disablement may only cancel scheduled future attempts while preserving all history.

question.prompt: How must endpoint signing secrets be created, stored, and disclosed? This determines whether users or operators can later recover a credential capable of forging webhooks.

options.label: Generated, shown once
options.description: Generate a high-entropy secret, disclose it only once at creation or rotation, store it encrypted with a managed KMS, never expose it through history or support tools, and allow only tenant admins or break-glass security operators to rotate or revoke it.

options.label: Generated, retrievable
options.description: Generate and encrypt the secret but allow authorized tenant admins to retrieve it later, simplifying setup recovery while increasing credential-exposure risk and audit scope.

options.label: Customer supplied
options.description: Require tenant admins to provide the secret, avoiding sender-side disclosure generation but permitting weak or reused credentials unless additional strength controls are imposed.

answer: Generate a cryptographically secure high-entropy secret for each endpoint. Disclose it only once to the tenant administrator at creation or rotation, with no later retrieval. Store it encrypted at rest using a managed KMS and restrict decryption to the signing service. Never expose the secret in delivery history, logs, support tools, or APIs. Only authorized tenant administrators or audited break-glass security operators may rotate or revoke it.

question.prompt: How must workers claim and recover attempts? This determines whether a crash or expired lease can cause duplicate HTTP requests while preventing a stale worker from overwriting the authoritative result.

options.label: Leased, fenced attempts
options.description: Atomically create and claim each attempt with an expiring lease and fencing token; reclaim expired work, permit duplicate sends after ambiguous crashes, and reject state updates from stale claimants.

options.label: Database lock per send
options.description: Hold a database lock throughout the outbound request, reducing concurrent execution but creating long transactions and still not eliminating ambiguity after network or process failure.

options.label: Queue visibility timeout
options.description: Rely on broker redelivery and visibility timeouts without persistent fencing, simplifying workers but allowing stale or concurrent consumers to race when recording outcomes.

answer: Use leased, fenced attempts. Atomically create and claim each attempt with a unique monotonically increasing fencing token and an expiring lease; only the current token holder may renew the lease or record the attempt outcome and delivery transition. Workers must renew leases while active. If a lease expires, atomically fence the stale claimant and recover the work. If persistence proves no HTTP send began, the same attempt may be reclaimed without consuming another attempt; otherwise record the attempt as an ambiguous worker-loss outcome that consumes its attempt number and, if the automatic six-attempt budget remains, create the next sequential retry attempt. A recovered worker may send a duplicate request after an ambiguous crash, consistent with at-least-once delivery, but any result or state update from its stale token must be rejected. Do not hold a database transaction open during the outbound request or rely on broker visibility timeouts as the authority.

question.prompt: What request and response data may delivery history expose? This determines whether operators can diagnose failures while preventing sensitive event payloads, signing data, and receiver content from leaking through the UI or support tools.

options.label: Redacted diagnostics
options.description: Persist encrypted request bytes for delivery, but show tenant admins metadata, hashes, sizes, timestamps, status, latency, retry reason, and a bounded sanitized response excerpt; support sees the same view with payload and response excerpts removed.

options.label: Tenant full payload
options.description: Allow tenant admins to reveal the exact request body and bounded response excerpt while support remains metadata-only, improving self-service debugging but increasing sensitive-data exposure and access-audit requirements.

options.label: Metadata only
options.description: Expose no request body or response body to any history user, minimizing leakage risk but making payload and receiver-error diagnosis substantially harder.

answer: Use redacted diagnostics. Persist the exact request bytes encrypted for sending and replay, but delivery history for tenant administrators may expose only metadata: event and delivery identifiers, endpoint identity, payload hash and byte size, timestamps, status, latency, attempt and replay classification, retry or terminal reason, and a bounded sanitized receiver-response excerpt. It must never expose the request body, signing secret, signature value, authorization data, or sensitive response content. Authorized support staff receive the same history with both payload content and response excerpts omitted. Sanitization and size bounds must be enforced before persistence or logging, and ordinary logs must contain only correlation IDs and non-sensitive metadata.

question.prompt: Which persistence authority should govern deliveries and replays? This determines uniqueness, crash-safe transitions, immutable history, and whether operators can distinguish the original delivery from each replay run.

options.label: Normalized immutable ledger
options.description: Persist event, endpoint delivery, replay run, and attempt as separate records; enforce one automatic delivery per tenant-event-endpoint, sequential unique attempt numbers per run, append-only attempts, and compare-and-set lifecycle transitions.

options.label: Mutable delivery aggregate
options.description: Store one delivery row with embedded or replaceable attempt state, reducing entities but weakening immutable audit history, replay separation, and concurrent fencing guarantees.

options.label: Event-sourced ledger
options.description: Persist every transition as an append-only domain event and derive current state through projections, providing strong auditability but adding substantial projection, migration, and operational complexity.

answer: Normalized immutable ledger. Persist the event, endpoint delivery, replay run, and each HTTP attempt as separate records. Enforce one automatic delivery per tenant-event-endpoint, unique sequential attempt numbers within each run, append-only immutable attempt history, and compare-and-set lifecycle transitions protected by lease fencing tokens. Manual replays create distinct runs linked to the original delivery and preserve the event ID without modifying prior records.

question.prompt: What maximum exact serialized JSON body size must be accepted? Because delivery fanout is atomic with the business event, this choice also determines whether an oversized payload rejects and rolls back the entire transaction or commits without webhook delivery.

options.label: 256 KiB, reject atomically
options.description: Limit the persisted UTF-8 envelope to 262,144 bytes and fail the complete business-event transaction before commit when exceeded; provides a clear no-gap guarantee with bounded storage and egress.

options.label: 1 MiB, reject atomically
options.description: Allow bodies up to 1,048,576 bytes and reject the complete transaction above that limit; supports richer events at greater storage, memory, bandwidth, and abuse cost.

options.label: Commit event, omit webhook
options.description: Commit the business event but record webhook fanout as rejected when oversized; preserves the business operation but breaks the guarantee that every accepted event atomically creates its eligible deliveries.

answer: Accept exact serialized UTF-8 JSON bodies up to and including 262,144 bytes. If the persisted envelope exceeds 262,144 bytes, reject it and roll back the entire business-event, outbox, and delivery-fanout transaction; do not commit the business event without its webhook deliveries.

question.prompt: What timeout limits must apply to every HTTP attempt? This determines when a slow or unreachable receiver produces an ambiguous retryable failure and constrains worker leases and delivery capacity.

options.label: 3s connect, 10s response
options.description: Allow at most 3 seconds for DNS-validated TCP/TLS connection establishment and 10 seconds from completed request transmission to receipt of the complete response; a timeout is retryable and redirects remain forbidden.

options.label: 5s connect, 30s response
options.description: Accommodate slower receivers but holds worker and connection capacity much longer during failures and delays retries.

options.label: 2s connect, 5s response
options.description: Fails fast and protects capacity, but may retry healthy receivers that have occasional network or processing latency.

answer: Apply a 3-second connection timeout and a 10-second response timeout to every HTTP attempt. The connection timeout covers DNS-validated TCP and TLS connection establishment. The response timeout runs from completion of request transmission until receipt of the complete response. Either timeout consumes the attempt and is retryable. Redirects remain forbidden.

question.prompt: How should an exhausted or permanently rejected delivery be represented and recovered? This determines whether terminal work remains solely in the immutable ledger or enters a separate operational queue.

options.label: Terminal ledger state
options.description: Mark the run terminally failed with its final reason, retain it in history, alert through metrics, and permit recovery only through a new authorized replay run; avoids a second source of truth.

options.label: Dead-letter queue
options.description: Copy terminal failures to a separate dead-letter queue for operator redrive, adding an operational recovery surface and reconciliation requirements with the immutable ledger.

options.label: Automatic slow retries
options.description: Continue periodic retries beyond the six-attempt budget, improving eventual recovery but contradicting the confirmed attempt limit and making terminal status indefinite.

answer: Terminal ledger state. Represent an exhausted delivery as failed_exhausted and a permanently rejected delivery as failed_permanent, recording the final sanitized reason in the immutable delivery, run, and attempt history. Emit metrics and alerts for terminal failures. Recovery is permitted only through a new authorized manual replay run linked to the original delivery; do not create a separate dead-letter queue or continue automatic retries beyond the six-attempt budget.

question.prompt: Which endpoint configuration may an authorized manual replay use? This determines whether replay can redirect an historical event to a destination that did not receive the original delivery.

options.label: Same endpoint, current config
options.description: Replay only through the original immutable endpoint ID using its current enabled URL and active secret, frozen when the replay starts; deleted or disabled endpoints cannot be replayed until restored or re-enabled.

options.label: Original snapshot

options.label: Any tenant endpoint

question.prompt: How should a newly created or destination-edited endpoint become eligible for fanout? This determines whether the platform may send production events before proving destination control and connectivity.

options.label: Verify before enabling
options.description: Create or edit the endpoint in a disabled pending-verification state, validate its public HTTPS destination, complete a signed challenge-response, and require a tenant admin to enable it; safest but adds onboarding steps.

options.label: Enable immediately
options.description: Allow an authorized tenant admin to activate the endpoint after synchronous URL and SSRF validation without proving destination control; simpler but may send sensitive events to a mistyped or unowned URL.

options.label: Optional verification
options.description: Let each tenant choose whether verification is required before activation; more flexible but expands policy, UI, support, and acceptance-test complexity.

answer: Verify before enabling. A newly created endpoint, or an endpoint whose destination URL is edited, enters a disabled pending_verification state and is ineligible for event fanout. The platform must first validate that the destination is public HTTPS under the established SSRF policy, then complete a signed challenge-response proving control and connectivity. After successful verification, an authorized tenant administrator must explicitly enable the endpoint. Editing the destination invalidates prior verification and disables the endpoint until the new destination is verified and re-enabled. No production webhook event may be sent to an endpoint while it is pending verification or disabled.

question.prompt: Which lifecycle model should be authoritative? This changes database transitions, history filters, cancellation semantics, and what support staff can reliably infer from each status.

options.label: Explicit state machines
options.description: Use distinct delivery/run states—pending, scheduled, in_progress, succeeded, failed_permanent, failed_exhausted, cancelled_endpoint_disabled—and immutable attempt outcomes such as succeeded, retryable_failure, permanent_failure, timeout, network_error, ambiguous_worker_loss, and cancelled; clearest operational contract at the cost of more states.

options.label: Compact shared states
options.description: Use pending, running, succeeded, failed, and cancelled for deliveries and replay runs, with detailed reasons only on attempts; simpler UI and storage but requires operators to interpret reason fields to distinguish permanent, exhausted, and ambiguous outcomes.

options.label: Derived status only
options.description: Persist immutable attempts and derive delivery and replay-run status dynamically; minimizes duplicated state but complicates queries, fencing transitions, alerts, and stable history semantics.

answer: Use explicit state machines. Delivery and replay-run states are pending, retry_scheduled, in_flight, succeeded, failed_permanent, failed_exhausted, and cancelled_endpoint_disabled. Attempt records are immutable and use explicit outcomes including succeeded, retryable_failure, permanent_failure, connect_timeout, response_timeout, network_error, TLS_failure, ambiguous_worker_loss, and cancelled_endpoint_disabled. Every transition records its reason and timestamp. Endpoint disablement changes only nonterminal scheduled work to cancelled_endpoint_disabled and preserves all prior delivery, run, and attempt history.

question.prompt: Which authentication and authorization model must govern the tenant REST API? This determines how every endpoint-management, history, secret, and replay operation is tenant-isolated and attributed to an actor.

options.label: Scoped OAuth + RBAC
options.description: Require OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens scoped to one tenant and enforce server-side roles and operation scopes, with privileged secret and replay actions requiring tenant-admin authority; strongest durable API contract with additional identity infrastructure.

options.label: Tenant API keys

answer: Scoped OAuth + RBAC. Require OAuth 2.0 bearer access tokens bound to exactly one tenant. Enforce tenant isolation server-side on every endpoint-management, verification, history, secret, and replay operation; never rely on client-supplied tenant identifiers for authorization. Tokens must carry explicit operation scopes, and server-side RBAC must map the authenticated actor to permitted tenant roles. Tenant-admin authority is required to create, edit, enable, disable, restore, or delete endpoints; rotate or revoke signing secrets; and initiate manual replays. Read-only tenant roles may access only the redacted history fields authorized for them. Support access uses separately issued tenant-scoped credentials: redacted history requires an authorized support role, while replay or secret intervention additionally requires the established break-glass authorization, recorded reason, and immutable actor-attributed audit record. Every mutating request and sensitive read must record the authenticated actor, tenant, token/client identity, granted role and scope, operation, target resource, timestamp, outcome, and correlation ID without recording bearer tokens, secrets, signatures, payloads, or sensitive response content. Missing, expired, incorrectly scoped, cross-tenant, or insufficient-role credentials must be rejected before resource details or state are disclosed or changed.

contract.summary: Design a production-ready, tenant-isolated webhook system providing signed immutable JSON delivery, at-least-once automatic retries, receiver deduplication, auditable history, and controlled manual replay. The emerging contract establishes transactional event fanout, stable Webhook-Id identity, versioned HMAC-SHA256 signing, frozen delivery configuration with explicit rotation exceptions, SSRF defenses, retry and worker recovery semantics, endpoint verification, encrypted persistence, redacted operator access, and a tenant REST API plus UI. The contract remains non-ready and implementation is not authorized because the listed material operational, API, quota, history, audit-retention, acceptance, and authorization decisions are still open.
confirmed_decisions: Delivery is at-least-once. Receivers deduplicate automatic attempts and manual replays by sender tenant plus immutable Webhook-Id for at least 30 days; duplicates remain possible after ambiguous failures.
Webhook-Id is preserved across endpoints, automatic attempts, endpoint changes, and manual replay. Sender delivery identity is separately keyed by event ID and endpoint ID.
The business event, outbox record, and complete eligible-endpoint delivery fanout are committed atomically in one datastore transaction; failure to persist the full fanout rolls back the transaction.

Each automatic delivery snapshots immutable endpoint ID, URL, and applicable configuration at event acceptance. Later changes affect new events only, except disablement cancels scheduled future attempts while preserving history.

Manual replay creates a distinct six-attempt run linked to the original delivery and event, targets only the original endpoint ID using its current enabled URL and active secret, and freezes that configuration at replay initiation.

Bodies are exact persisted UTF-8 JSON bytes using a stable envelope with id, type, version, occurred_at, account_id, and data. Incompatible event payload changes require a new integer version scoped to the event type.
The maximum body size is 262,144 bytes inclusive. Oversized bodies reject and roll back the complete business-event and fanout transaction.
Requests use HTTPS and expose Webhook-Id, Webhook-Timestamp, and Webhook-Signature. The signature header contains comma-separated v1=<lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256> entries.

HMAC input is the exact bytes Webhook-Id + period + base-10 Unix-seconds Webhook-Timestamp + period + exact transmitted body. Bodies are not reserialized or content-encoded, and header values are not normalized.

Each attempt receives a fresh timestamp and signature. Receivers reject timestamps more than 300 seconds from their clock and accept when any v1 signature matches any accepted secret using constant-time comparison.

Signing secrets are cryptographically generated, shown once to tenant administrators, encrypted through managed KMS, decryptable only by the signing service, and never exposed through APIs, logs, history, or support tools.

Normal rotation has a 24-hour receiver verification overlap without dual-signing. Newly started attempts use only the new active secret, including attempts whose delivery snapshot names the old version.
Emergency compromise revokes the secret without overlap, pauses new attempts, cancels scheduled future attempts, and requires an authorized replacement-secret activation before delivery resumes.
Endpoints permit public HTTPS destinations only. Every connection re-resolves DNS, rejects non-public addresses, connects only to the validated address, and never follows redirects.
New or destination-edited endpoints remain disabled and pending verification until SSRF validation, signed challenge-response, and explicit tenant-admin enablement succeed.
A delivery has at most six automatic attempts. Retry delays are 10, 30, 120, 600, and 3600 seconds after attempts one through five.
Connection refusal, DNS failure, connect timeout, TLS failure, response timeout, HTTP 408, 425, 429, and 5xx are retryable. Other 4xx and redirects are terminal. Complete 2xx responses succeed.
For HTTP 429 or 503, a valid Retry-After between 1 and 3600 seconds replaces the normal delay; otherwise the normal delay applies.
Every attempt has a 3-second DNS-validated TCP/TLS connection timeout and a 10-second complete-response timeout measured after request transmission.
Delivery is unordered and concurrent; receivers cannot rely on arrival order.
Workers use expiring leases and monotonically increasing fencing tokens. Stale claimants cannot update state. Ambiguous worker loss consumes an attempt and may cause duplicate transmission.

Event, endpoint delivery, replay run, and attempt are separate normalized records. Automatic delivery uniqueness is tenant-event-endpoint; attempts have unique sequential numbers per run and immutable append-only history.

Delivery and replay-run states are pending, retry_scheduled, in_flight, succeeded, failed_permanent, failed_exhausted, and cancelled_endpoint_disabled. Attempts record explicit immutable outcomes and transition reasons with timestamps.
Terminal failures remain ledger states rather than entering a dead-letter queue. Recovery occurs only through an authorized new replay run.

Encrypted payloads and operational delivery, attempt, and replay records are retained for 90 days. Payload bytes are then irreversibly deleted and replay is disabled; payload-free immutable audit records remain separately governed.

Tenant history exposes identifiers, endpoint identity, payload hash and size, timestamps, status, latency, attempt/replay classification, reasons, and a bounded sanitized response excerpt. It never exposes bodies, secrets, signatures, authorization data, or sensitive receiver content.
Support history omits payload content and response excerpts. Sanitization and bounds apply before persistence or logging; ordinary logs contain only correlation IDs and non-sensitive metadata.

Tenant administrators may view and replay their tenant's deliveries. Support may view tenant-scoped redacted history; support replay requires break-glass authorization, a reason, and immutable actor-attributed audit.
The management surface is a versioned tenant REST API plus a UI using that contract.

Management authentication uses OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens bound to one tenant, explicit operation scopes, and server-side RBAC. Cross-tenant and insufficiently authorized requests are rejected before disclosure or mutation.
Tenant-admin authority is required for endpoint lifecycle changes, secret rotation or revocation, and replay. Read-only roles receive only their authorized redacted history fields.
Sensitive reads and mutations audit actor, tenant, client identity, role, scope, operation, target, timestamp, outcome, and correlation ID without recording credentials or sensitive content.

Manual replay rate limits and any remaining immutable audit fields
Observability, alert thresholds, and delivery SLOs

acceptance_checks: Not sealable yet: define tests proving atomic business-event and complete fanout commit or rollback, including oversized payload rejection.
Define tests proving stable body bytes and Webhook-Id across automatic attempts and replay, fresh per-attempt timestamps, and byte-exact HMAC verification.
Define tests proving lost acknowledgements and ambiguous worker crashes may repeat requests while fenced stale workers cannot overwrite authoritative state.
Define the full outcome matrix for 2xx, redirects, terminal 4xx, retryable status codes, Retry-After bounds, DNS/TLS/network failures, and both timeout classes.
Define tests for the six-attempt budget and exact retry schedule, including terminal failed_permanent and failed_exhausted states.

Define tests proving destination edits cannot redirect queued automatic deliveries, disablement cancels only future scheduled work, and replay uses frozen current configuration for the original endpoint.

Define security tests for public-HTTPS enforcement, prohibited address ranges, DNS rebinding, per-attempt revalidation, redirect refusal, tenant isolation, role/scope enforcement, and pre-disclosure authorization failure.
Define rotation and revocation tests covering the 24-hour verification overlap, active-key-only attempt signing, no dual-sign requirement, immediate emergency revocation, pause, and audited recovery.
Define retention and redaction tests proving one-time secret disclosure, KMS-protected storage, sensitive-data exclusion, 90-day payload deletion, replay expiry, and separately retained audits.
Define endpoint lifecycle tests for pending verification, signed challenge-response, explicit enablement, edit-triggered invalidation, disablement, deletion, restoration, and replay eligibility.

Define history and replay API acceptance checks after pagination, filters, status presentation, idempotency, validation errors, rate limits, quotas, compatibility, and audit-retention decisions are confirmed.
Define load, fairness, observability, alerting, and SLO acceptance checks after concurrency, quota, abuse-control, and service-level decisions are confirmed.
